analysis.one_liner: Requires minimum nurse and caregiver staffing levels at Medicare and Medicaid nursing homes.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote in either committee and died when the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required nursing homes that receive Medicare or Medicaid money to keep a licensed nurse on duty for every 15 to 30 residents depending on the shift, and one direct caregiver for every 5 to 15 residents. It would have barred counting administrators or kitchen and housekeeping staff toward those ratios, required full-time directors of nursing at each facility, and forced facilities to post their actual daily staffing levels where residents and families could see them. It also extended nursing home quality and staffing rules to every resident, not just those whose care Medicare or Medicaid pays for.
analysis.who_benefits: Nursing home residents and their families, who would get more hands-on care and the ability to check staffing levels on a posted notice; and direct care workers, including certified nurse aides and licensed nurses, who would work in better-staffed facilities.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Nursing home residents and direct care workers

how_it_helps.text: Sets specific shift-by-shift staffing minimums: one licensed nurse per 15 residents by day and one direct caregiver per 5 residents by day, loosening only at night, and bars counting anyone doing non-caregiving work like food preparation or administration toward the ratio [S3].

Requires facilities to post, in each resident area, the current resident-to-nurse and resident-to-caregiver ratios, the names and titles of caregivers on duty, and the number of residents, with records kept for two years [S3].
Extends all nursing home quality-of-care protections to every resident of a Medicare- or Medicaid-certified facility, regardless of who pays for the resident's care [S3].
Includes payment adjustments so Medicare and Medicaid rates would rise to reflect the cost of meeting the new staffing requirements, rather than leaving facilities to absorb them entirely [S3].
Directs the Secretary of Health and Human Services to report within one year on whether enough trained caregiving personnel exist to meet the requirements and how to attract and retain them [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Nursing home operators face hiring and compliance costs, though the bill adjusts Medicare and Medicaid payments to reflect those costs, meaning federal and state taxpayers ultimately bear much of the added program spending.

drawbacks.text: The staffing mandate is expensive: the bill explicitly raises Medicare and Medicaid payment rates to cover the cost of meeting the new ratios, shifting added costs to federal and state budgets and taxpayers [S3].

The bill itself directs a study of whether enough trained nurses and aides exist to fill the new positions, acknowledging that a nationwide staffing floor could run into workforce shortages and require new recruitment and retention efforts [S3].

Facilities with fewer than 100 beds get some flexibility (part-time assistant directors and supervisors), but small operators still face full-time director-of-nursing and ratio requirements along with new recordkeeping and posting duties [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core tradeoff is real: more staff per resident measurably improves care and safety, but it costs money, and this bill chose to pay for it through higher Medicare and Medicaid rates rather than forcing facilities to absorb it alone. That makes the burden fall partly on taxpayers instead of entirely on an industry that had long kept staffing thin to hold down costs. The posting requirements cost little and give families direct visibility into whether a facility is actually staffed. On balance the bill was a straightforward consumer-safety measure with an honest funding mechanism, weakened mainly by the open question of workforce supply that the bill itself flagged.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to two House committees and then to a Health subcommittee, and neither committee ever took it up, so it died quietly when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jan Schakowsky introduced the bill on November 16, 2001, joined by seven original cosponsors including Reps. Henry Waxman and Bernie Sanders [S3].
The Speaker referred it to both the Ways and Means Committee and the Energy and Commerce Committee on the day it was introduced [S5].
On December 10, 2001, it was referred to the Health subcommittee, where consideration is at the discretion of the chairman [S5].
No hearing, markup, or floor vote ever followed, and the bill accumulated 17 cosponsors, all Democrats plus the chamber's one Independent, before the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003 [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nursing home operators benefited from avoiding the staffing mandate and its costs; residents and caregivers gained nothing because the bill never advanced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Nursing home operators, whose costs stayed down

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no roll calls exist; its 17 cosponsors were all Democrats plus the chamber's lone Independent, with no Republican support recorded [S4].

industries.note: The bill would have forced operators to hire many more licensed nurses and aides and add full-time nursing administrators, raising operating costs. It offset much of that by raising Medicare and Medicaid payment rates, but operators' underlying interest in the bill ran against residents, since thin staffing is how facilities hold down labor costs.

The bill would have created demand for licensed nurses and certified nurse aides and improved working conditions in understaffed facilities. It also directed a federal report on how to attract and retain caregiving staff.
